Vignette:
# Kofi's Vigil

Kofi Mensah had spent forty-two years with the Coast Guard, most of them at the station in Mobile Bay, where the water was brown and the air carried the industrial smell of the refineries inland. He had been a good officer—meticulous about protocol, steady under pressure, the kind of man younger recruits asked for advice. His wife, Ama, had raised their three children in a modest house three miles from the base, and for decades, Kofi had moved between those two worlds with a kind of equilibrium that felt natural, almost invisible to him.

On a March morning in 2019, Kofi was conducting a routine inspection of a cargo vessel that had docked to transfer chemicals. He was fifty-eight then, still fit, still sharp. The ship's manifest listed industrial solvents—nothing unusual for Mobile. He was walking the deck with the captain when a valve coupling on the transfer line suddenly failed. Kofi remembered the sound first: a metallic shriek, then a hiss that turned into a roar. The liquid that sprayed out was colorless but acrid, and within seconds it had soaked his uniform and his skin. He remembered the burning—not sharp, but deep and creeping, as though the chemical were dissolving something inside his chest. He remembered stumbling backward, his eyes streaming, and then the chaos of emergency protocols: the alarm, the shouting, the way his vision blurred and narrowed until he was pulled away by other officers and rushed to the decontamination unit.

The hospital kept him for three days. The doctors said he had been fortunate—the exposure was significant but not catastrophic. His lungs would recover. His skin would heal. They sent him home with instructions and reassurance. But something had fractured in Kofi that day, something the doctors could not see or measure.

Within weeks, the memories began to replay without warning. He would be sitting at the dinner table, and suddenly he was back on that deck—the hiss of the valve, the acrid smell filling his nostrils, the burning sensation spreading across his chest and arms as if it were happening again in real time. The memories came with a vividness that was almost photographic; he could see the exact angle of the sunlight on the water, the expression on the captain's face, the rust stain on the coupling. When these moments came, they overwhelmed him completely. He would have to leave the table, leave the room, because the emotion that accompanied the memory was so intense that he felt as though he might break apart if he stayed present with it. Ama learned not to ask what was wrong. She learned that he needed to be left alone until the episode passed.

The silence in their home had become a different kind of problem. Kofi had come to believe that quiet meant danger—that when nothing was happening, something terrible was gathering. He found himself listening constantly, his body tensed, waiting for the sound that would confirm his fear. Even inside his own house, with Ama reading beside him and the television off, he felt as though he were still on high alert, as though the next moment might bring another catastrophe. His heart would race at the smallest unexpected sound: a door closing, a car in the driveway, the furnace kicking on. His hands would shake. Sweat would bead on his forehead.

He had retired from the Coast Guard at sixty-five, hoping that distance from the base would help. It did not. Instead, he had become someone who could not tolerate even minor disruptions—a change in plans, a disagreement with Ama, a news story about an industrial accident. These small upsets would trigger a cascade of panic and despair, and he was certain that if he allowed himself to think directly about what had happened on that ship, he would be unable to function at all. So he did not think about it. He did not speak about it. He did not visit the base or answer calls from old colleagues. He had come to see the world as fundamentally dangerous, a place where invisible threats could emerge at any moment and change everything.

It was Ama who finally insisted he see someone. She had watched her husband withdraw, watched him become a man who sat in their living room with his shoulders tensed and his eyes scanning the room as though searching for an exit. She had felt him flinch in his sleep, heard him call out in voices she did not recognize. After a particularly bad night—when Kofi had woken in a panic, convinced that someone was breaking into the house—she had made the appointment herself and driven him to the clinic. Kofi sat in the waiting room, seventy-two years old now, his hands folded in his lap, afraid that speaking about what happened would destroy what little equilibrium he had left, but more afraid of what he was becoming in the silence.
